utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have half an hour to 40 minutes left with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you, Mr. May, to extend my time a little bit, because in the meantime, I received some information, because people have been reacting to this testimony, and it can be easily shown that this witness absolutely is not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see how we get on. But at the moment, it's 30 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should say this: The transcript is not working at the moment. A transcript is being taken, but it's not running on our screens, and that's why you're getting it blank. It will apparently be repaired, it's hoped, by the break. We don't want to hold up the trial. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you presented inaccurate information regarding the activities of your unit, I have several questions in connection with that. Do you know that in your unit during 1998 and 1999, 63 members of this unit were killed and 300 were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about a small number who got killed, not a number that big, no. And the troops were getting killed for no good reason whatsoever on our side. And as for the KLA, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know what this means that "the troops were being killed for no good reason whatsoever." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I explain this to you? For example, I know of a particular case when soldiers were driving in a military vehicle and then one soldier got killed by another soldier. His rifle went off and killed him by hitting him in the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You explained that, that soldiers were being killed because of the poor organisation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm telling you that 63 were killed and 300 were wounded. Are you trying to say that these were not casualties due to combat but that it happened due to poor organisation, that they killed each other and wounded each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this figure that you've given, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There are official data to prove this. However, do you know that in the area that this unit was in, that is to say Prizren, Suva Reka, Orahovac, and Djakovica, 230 soldiers and 72 members of the police got killed in combat with the KLA and in the bombing, and 538 were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know, in connection with those lootings, and you said that you took part in them as well because you were seizing goods from shops without paying these goods. You said that you did that too; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that proceedings are under way before the military court in Nis against 45 members of your unit and the entire brigade? As for the entire brigade, it's over 300. And two are being tried for murder.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, there is a list here, a list of persons submitted to the Court in relation to what this witness has been speaking about. This testifies to the fact that he has not been saying the truth, and I would like to have this admitted into evidence, if you want to take it, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the list be produced. Yes. It can be shown to the Prosecution. Yes, we'll go on and the Prosecution can have a look at that. Mr. Usher, if you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the two prisoners, do you know that in addition to having civilian trousers that they had KLA uniforms on the upper part, also flak jackets and automatic rifles, vests and also ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that. They had jackets on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What you did see or what you did not see is something that we explained last time. Do you know that the house that was hit by a tank in the village of Mece, as you described it, was not in the village of Mece at all? It was at the entrance into the village of Granovik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I showed the house and they said it was the village of Mece.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who said that to you? How come? Where's the house? How do you know about all of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there. I've been telling you that very nicely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this house was turned into a bunker and on the northern side it had sandbags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the other side it had a trench that was dug and from that house the KLA kept under fire the police checkpoint and the bridge. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that's what it says in the official reports, Mr. K32?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that you've got everything, don't you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the fighting in the village of Mece went on for three days and that the KLA attacked from position 385 from Rakovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I do know that we were there for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that anybody got killed? For example, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a policeman was wounded. Whether he was killed, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The name of the policeman is Lilic. He's from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he got killed, but anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must pause, both of you, between question and answer. Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you claim that you were listening to various communications, how were these communications upheld?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: By radio transmitters, the small ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. And I have information here stating that radio communications were forbidden and that communications were only going through the local PTT cable and the relay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then -- well, I was only blind and deaf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that because you look very healthy to me. It must have been a different reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness K32, now, you may find it irritating to be asked these questions, but nonetheless, can I remind you you're in a court. Just answer them. If you disagree or if it's not true what is being put to you, just say it's not true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What was the code that the brigade commander used when you listened to him speaking? You said that it was by way of a radio transmitter, whatever. What was his code? Did he use his name and surname or did he use a code name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A code name. A code name. There is also a password for this but I can't remember the password.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the password.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you can't remember what he used but you remember what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, so many years have gone by. I can't remember every little detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your father who came to visit you in Nis and who then took you to the army was involved in transferring Albanians to Plav and then towards Italy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he took money for this endeavour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is information about this, data to prove it. And is it correct, Mr. K32, that the main link was a certain Bujevic, sorry, Rujevic with a "R," Rujevic, a tinsmith from Pec whose nickname was Bajo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was staying with you during the NATO address while his brother was in Pec throughout and later on got a job with the UNMIK police in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that they tried to get you to testify here in order to settle your accounts and so that they would forgive you your debts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is precisely this Rujevic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. Right. Okay. You said that the terrorists were not very well-armed and that they had hunting guns for the most part.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did see one hunting gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please take a look at the information contained here, what was seized at the state border, May 1998, December 1998. I'm going to submit this into evidence. It only refers to this unit. Let me just quote a few items from this list. Automatic rifles, 762, Chinese made, 418 of them. Semi-automatic rifles, Chinese made, 453. Ammunition, for example. There are different items here. There are a hundred items. But ammunition, 114.550 pieces. Then in boxes in crates, how many hundreds of crates. Albanian ammunition of different calibres. 111.152, et cetera, et cetera. Mortar mines, 60 millimetre, 117 cumulative mines, Chinese made, 271, et cetera, et cetera. Bullets for 127 heavy machine-gun Browning, and then another heavy machine-gun, 10.000, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer, Mr. Milosevic. Witness K32 -- Just a moment. Witness K32, do you know anything about this list which is being read out or anything about these type of arms for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that we found weapons. What Mr. Milosevic mentioned, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please take this into evidence and also as proof that the witness is not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is matter of comment and that will be for us to decide, but we will certainly take the document. Show it, please, to the Prosecution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many times in March and April 1999 were you at Vrbnica, the Vrbnica border crossing, and what business did you have there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Vrbnica border post?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few times. A few times. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We were talking about the village of Mece. And tell me now, you say that your combat group was the second combat group and that it was in the village of Damjane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the village of Damjane was the 3rd combat group, not the 2nd combat group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know it was the 2nd combat group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Where were the troops put up in the village of Damjane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In houses, in abandoned houses and in the schools too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Damjane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I know, it is correct that the army were staying in the cooperative building outside the village and also in metal containers that were placed to the north.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In those containers, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also put up in containers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you were they were put up in containers and you said it was in the school and houses, and now you're saying, yes, in the cooperative and in the containers the way I put it. So this is completely different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the schools and in the houses and in the containers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Since you say that the army was in Albanian territory, two kilometres into Albanian territory, were you ever at the border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were the border buildings in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was they border post myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if these buildings, these huts at the border were right in front of you and if you were facing Albania, how were you then in the territory of Albania itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that soldiers told me that they got into Albanian territory, two kilometres into Albanian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, somebody got in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not that what I'm claiming. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many persons got killed from the ranks of this 3rd combat unit in the village of Damjane, from your unit in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One person got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of that soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Petar Markovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the other two soldiers who also got killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know, as concerns one of them, that a container fell, toppled, and killed him that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you see Colonel Delic while the fighting was going on near Retimlje and Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because there was no fighting in your area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do not have information about the soldiers who were killed. You have no information about the members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to tender a list of soldiers who were killed in this area that this protected witness of yours, K32, has been testifying about. There's also a list of members of the Ministry of the Interior who got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you stated that an NCO, together with his soldiers, killed about 15 civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of this non-commissioned officer and what unit did he come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me what his name was if you mentioned his name in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: His name was Rajko? And do you know that everybody wants to testify about the fact that you lied about this killing of a civilian and that that is a notorious lie?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is a comment, as you know. Now, you can put to him, if you want, that his evidence isn't true and then he can answer it, but running comments of that sort do not help and are not permissible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's suggested is that you haven't told the truth about the killing of the civilian by the NCO. Now, you can answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the truth about the murder of those civilians. That's the truth. And there are more witness who is can testify to that, people who were together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, Mr. K32, explained that approximately in this way, if I remember correctly and if I made correct notes on Wednesday, they killed a mother and her baby and 13 or 15 civilians, that all soldiers were shooting, that you were there and that everybody was shooting except for you. You were the only one who wasn't shooting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shooting too, but not at the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. You were everywhere and you heard Delic everywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear Delic then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you said that on orders, you set a house on fire. Is that correct? And then you were asked how you set that house on fire. Do you know that you disappointed them a great deal when you said you used a lighter, because we have heard here many times that there were special rifles for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used a lighter to torch that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that you saw that murder, this assassination of the 15 civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I was close by. However, I saw another five persons who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a second. You claim that you took part in this killing of those 15 civilians with a proviso that you were not shooting at them. You say that you were shooting at the roof.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I didn't say that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said I was close by, and I was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look, did you see the murder of those 15 civilians or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw dead civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw dead civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say you saw dead civilians, which means you didn't see their killing. How can you claim then that you know who killed them? You know the name of the sergeant when you didn't see the incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the sergeant and his soldiers there, so it means that it was them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's your conclusion based on that -- I see. Could then somebody else come to the conclusion that it was you who killed them since you were there and you were seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I happened to be there, somebody could conclude that I killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't kill them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say they killed them. I saw they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were close by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that they were exactly there where those people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I see -- I think that this matter is now clear. Let's go on. You said on the 4th of March you were quartered in the village of Trnje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, on the 24th. I had heard you saying the 4th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until the 25th of March, in the area of Trnje village, there was no police or army units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were on the 24th. Oh, I'm sorry. On the 24th, the bombing started, which means we left our barracks on the 24th, and on the 25th we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So now you agree with what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness said on the 25th of March, in his evidence, about Trnje that he received an order to go there to cleanse the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the operation near Retimlje and Studencane when you were in Trnje village, did somebody from your brigade get killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear about the deaths of three soldiers, Slobodan Gasparic, Bojo Jovanovic, and Vladimir Mirkov, and eight other soldiers who were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't? Did you hear about two MUP members that were killed, Ivica Spasic and Zeljko Kirkner, and seven wounded policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, you were a soldier. Are you familiar with the rules of the service of the army of Yugoslav, being a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a soldier, during your training you had to be familiarised with the rules of your service.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that those rules of service set out very clearly that a soldier must not execute an order which constitutes a crime, a criminal offence, and must instead inform his superior officer about such orders, somebody superior to the person who issued the order in the first place. Do you know about this rule?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you were constantly in the vicinity of Delic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were a driver, who were the drivers? What were the names of the drivers who served Delic in 1998, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was from Bijelo Polje, and I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. What was the name of the driver of Delic's who was wounded during the attack of Albanian terrorists on the vehicle? Do you remember at least that? He was a colleague of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the driver was -- was wounded while I was on record as a deserter. That was the first driver who was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how come that your unit was able to shoot at Jeskovo village when from their position, they couldn't even see the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could. They could. It's a village situated in a depression. There are no more than 15 houses in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here you have a map indicating those positions, including a legend. You can see Jeskovo village there and you can put it also on the ELMO, if you wish, of course, to use it. Do you have any idea how much ammunition you spent when you were shooting for half an hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go back to this map. If it goes on the overhead projector, we can all see it. Yes. Mr. Milosevic, what's the point about this map, what it shows?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that the position of his unit was such that they were unable to even see the Jeskovo village from it. And secondly -- but I'll ask him about it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since all the terrorists were wearing uniforms and were well-armed, where did you see civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them moving around the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's stay with this map for a moment. We've got it here. Mr. Milosevic, where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got it from my associates or, rather, through my associates from Belgrade over the weekend. I got it this morning, rather, because I can't see my associates during the weekend, according to your rules. I got this map this morning, and it was drafted by competent people who have in their position official data about the events concerned. And all data indicate that this witness is not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You said that. Now, we can see a marking with "Delic" on it. Is that where the unit was supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it is described on the map, that is the real situation. That is the reality concerning the positions of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can see the village above where Delic is supposed to be, Jeskovo. Now, can the witness help us with this: Does that set out the position as you remember it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This map is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us what the real position or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The real position -- that was -- that was it, not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was where Delic was, and we were around here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And did you go into the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did. We did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let that also be exhibited. It may be sensible to have some numbers. I will ask the Registrar to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I just might at this point: We've been shown a series of some three other sets of documents and then this map. No problem with the map, but with the other documents, I want to point out that, A, they're not translated; B, they were not shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll admit them subject to objection in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could they perhaps be marked for identification? Especially the first document. It appears to be something that should be shown during the part of the Defence case. I mean, I don't really object to them, I just don't know what they are. And they weren't shown to the witness. Their probative value certainly has not been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, show them, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll mark them for identification, and the map we'll mark as an exhibit. In due course they can be established or not. I don't think there's much point showing them to the witness; they're simply lists. Yes, let's go on in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first list, Your Honours, will be marked for identification as Exhibit D23, the second list will be marked for identification as D24, and the third list will be marked for identification as D25, and the map will be marked as D26.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So I assert that all the terrorists were wearing uniforms and were well-armed. And I'm asking you, where did you see civilians, in view of the fact that, according to my information, the civilians were located in villages Lodja, Zagradska, Biluca and Pociste and nobody ever touched them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never -- I don't remember ever saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying you stated that. I'm saying that that is my information, whereas you say that you had seen civilians there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was the entire event monitored by OSCE representatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't monitor it because we didn't allow them to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that three OSCE vehicles were present there from 9.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were at the entrance to the village and the army didn't let them go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean they were not on the site where the immediate shooting took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But how did you see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were withdrawing, retreating, Mr. Milosevic, we saw them parked as an intersection far away from the village, and the army wouldn't let them pass further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know the army didn't let them pass any further? Because in my report it says that the precise event that you describe was attended by three OSCE vehicles and representatives from 9.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know more about it, Mr. Milosevic, than you do because I was there, and what your report says is not true. I understand that you are defending yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not go into whether you understand me or not. It's quite obvious that you don't -- you're not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the truth and the whole truth. Let those people confirm that the army wouldn't let them pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim, on page 6, in paragraph 2 of your statement that you were ordered, when the NATO bombing started, to mop up Albanian villages and to order everyone to leave Kosovo and go to Albania. That is what you write. But you say in essence most of those people were actually killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't state that, but that's what it was like. That's what happened. Unless you did something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't add anything to your statement. On page 6, it says: "We were told that an order had been issued to mop up, to clear out Albanian villages and tell everyone to leave Kosovo and go to Albania, but in practice, most of those people were killed." So were you or were you not telling the truth when you said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they actually noted, but what I said was that villages which were evacuated where people were expelled in Kosovo -- how shall I explain this? Everybody was driven out, told to go to Albania. We had orders to expel all civilians and drive them towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you get an order to the effect that you should drive everyone out and tell them to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have such orders. I didn't receive them personally, but the army did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, but you were part of that army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the order being issued to drive people out to Albania?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who issued the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those NCOs of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the given your statement you said: "Delic said that those people should be removed from the village and that he's not interested in where they were going to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are now using the statement about the period before the bombing or about the period during the bombing, and you are confusing me by jumping from one to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point that he makes, so you can understand it, is this: that Delic's order was given in an earlier period. The period that you were asking him about is the period of the NATO bombing, and what he complains of is that by jumping from one to the other you're confusing him. The Court can understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. So your NCO told them to drive them out to Albania?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you expelled them and saw them off too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an eyewitness to an incident where a woman was told to go to Albania, and we killed her father, her grandfather, and her brother. I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you escorted those villagers from the village to the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't escort them. We just told them to go away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just told them to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had no need to escort them because they had company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that basically most of those people were killed, that's what you said. So who went to Albania if most of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, when the bombing started, Mr. Milosevic, the first five days, killings took place in villages where I was. And later, I would run into columns of people who were forced to go to Albania. They didn't go there of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand now. Columns of people filed away to Albania. How could they have formed columns if you said you killed most of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't kill all of them. We didn't kill all of them. A small part of them was killed in the first five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it is your assertion that most of them were killed and a small number were sent to Albania.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my assertion. I said something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep confusing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've now had the 40 minutes allotted. We will give you another ten. If you ask too many questions of a witness, he will become inevitably confused, particularly if you put confusing things to him. So keep it separate, these questions, and keep them clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I was asking very clear questions, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you were not being very clear, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 6, in paragraph 2, you say -- however, before that, you said that you had said something different. Those were your words. What was it you said actually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not in any paragraph, but when I asked you whether it was your assertion that most of those people were killed and a small part of them was expelled to Albania, so those are two versions --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are not versions, Mr. Milosevic. In the first -- we are talking now about the time of the bombing. In the first five days, there were killings of civilians in villages. Five days later, we retreated to our barracks, and it is common knowledge who issued orders to people to leave their villages and go to Albania. That's the PJP, the special police units. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You say that when you entered the village, you split up into teams. Give me the names of the soldiers who were in your team.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your team, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you their names. I can't give you their names. They will come here and sit in this chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in every house certain groups of soldiers killed people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. They didn't come there for no purpose at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army killed people, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that all the inhabitants of the village of Medevce were killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, all of them, all that we found there. Mr. Milosevic, one thing; I meant Trnje village in the context of what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean all the locals of Trnje village were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all who were there when we got in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that happened when you split up into groups and killed them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They tried to run across the fields and run away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you talk about dead bodies, you say that you saw five dead bodies which you went somewhere to bury.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not above the village but away from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say five people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not five people, five women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Five women? You said that they were buried precisely by those who killed them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were with us. They were watching us bury them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just check this in your statement, because this is the first time I hear you mention five women. I want to see if that's what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here you say on page 7: "We drove to the far end of the village." The captain ordered you to collect the bodies of women and children and the elderly. "However, the bodies of the children and most of the women were no longer there."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you mention these five bodies. So if that was indeed the way it happened, how come you had only five people killed? If that was such a mass killing with teams romping around the village and killing people all day, how come there were only five?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we only found there three elderly men and five women. And before we came, somebody took away the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't you think this -- please look at this part of your statement. It is good for the public to hear this, although they can't see your face. You say on page 6: "There were no incidents of rape..." You say, "There were no incidents of rape, but only because there was no time for that. Had there been time, that would have occurred too."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It surely would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about rapes? Had there been any rapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any, but if we had had time, there would have been rapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please explain. How did you come to the conclusion that something that never happened would have happened had there been time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll just pause one moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic, a soldier who killed a young girl in that same village, one soldier whose last name was Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say I was there too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was from Kosovo himself. He moaned and cried because he had killed her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean he cried because --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because "I didn't get to rape her first." He killed her before she was raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that some soldiers were with you from Montenegro. Tell me the names of those soldiers from Montenegro so that we can hear from them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know them or do you know --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, but I don't want to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's your obligation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not my obligation, because one of those soldiers is supposed to come here and sit in this chair too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us at least his name, the one who is coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have to say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness declines to do so. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've got about a minute more, so that's time for two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the end, you were saying, and I have to skip a lot of questions here, but ultimately it doesn't really matter because everything is pretty obvious here. You were asked towards the examination-in-chief about your discussions with the commander whom you drove to various meetings. And in response to that, you answered that you really didn't talk to him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't talk to him much, but I'm not deaf, and from what he did say I could get an inkling into his thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you didn't talk to him, how could you make any conclusions? Did he talk to himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point he said all of those people should be driven out of this country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard him say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that. And in reply to that, I said, "Yes. Yes, of course."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And whom did he mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me, did you discuss that with other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have the amicus any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just a couple, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, it's been suggested that you've been lying to this Court. Would there be any benefit or any gain to you for coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you put that in clearer terms? I didn't really...

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Why are you here to testify? How did you come to come to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How I did it? Well, let me tell you concretely first and foremost. These women I buried, that we buried, until I spoke of this, I could not get any peaceful sleep. Do you see what I'm saying? That was my objective. And to say all the rest. So that means, you know, these five women that we buried, this tortured me for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Is there any benefit, any gain to you personally for coming here to testify? Did anyone promise you anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I have no benefit. The only benefit is that my conscience is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness K32, thanks to the summary offered by the Prosecutor, I notice that you took some investigators to the place where you took the bodies of five women. Did you take them also to the place where you buried them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when we set out, they told me that they had found that immediately and that there was no need for that. So we went elsewhere. The man who was there, he knew about it already. He just asked me to tell him which house they were from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K32, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Wait for the blinds to be drawn up. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of administrative matters that it would be convenient to address now, given that we lost time last week and that presently we're scheduled to include sittings on this Friday. I have to make it plain that we have more evidence available for this week than can sensibly be accommodated within the week, and indeed one of the things I'm going to ask the Chamber to at least consider is the possibility of extending the sittings into next week should that be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Arrangements have already been made. That is to be part of the preparation time for the next part of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So be it. Then if we can start -- to help the Chamber with its understanding of the decisions I have to make about evidence to be called, if we can start with K34, for whom particular arrangements have, of course, been made. It's very desirable that he should be concluded this week. Indeed, I make that something of a priority. If we allow two days and perhaps one session for him, then that would mean we should start his evidence in the last session on Wednesday. Advancing that notional start time, if there's any matters that have to be taken on Thursday or Friday. The other most substantial witness listed for this week, of course, was K33. He's here. The Chamber has had submitted by him a paper drafted, I think, by his lawyer and with a translation, and I think that the amici have just recently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't had that. Nothing from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It came directly to Your Honour on the 19th of July in a letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, I have you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That identifies an issue that he wants to raise. Really it's an issue between him, I think, and the Chamber, given that he's a witness here under subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If I'm thinking of the right matter, we've made an order in relation to it. But we may be talking eliptically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The letter of the 19th of July, or the document of the 19th of July from K33 explains his difficulties in giving evidence in the absence of the lifting of restrictions on his speaking about state and federal secrets. If you haven't seen it, then you obviously should see it. It has a Registry number on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It has got lost in the system. It's somewhere in the system. No doubt it's going around the building, but it hasn't come to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm alarmed that this has happened. Let me explain the position, and K33 knows that I'm going to explain the position and to do so publicly. K33 is the pseudonym for Mr. Lilic, the former president of Yugoslavia, who is here under a subpoena to give evidence and is happy that his name should be known. Happy that it should be known once the time came for him to give evidence, although I gather, as has been happening from time to time, the local newspapers have published this information and indeed published his pseudonym in breach of all sorts of obvious orders of this Court. His concern, and he would like to address the Chamber about it directly himself, is that he is at present in the position of not being able to give evidence about facts or about documents that constitute state or federal secrets without being at risk himself. And his document submitted on the 19th of July deals with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At risk from whom, Mr. Nice? At risk from --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Prosecution in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By the national authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the national authorities. Various steps have been taken since he was first in contact with the Office of the Prosecutor. Various steps have been taken to relieve him of that risk, and it's been a long process and it is only just coming to some conclusion now. But it is not completely resolved, and until it is completely resolved, there would be severe limitations on the evidence that Mr. Lilic can give if he is to be free of the liability and risk that understandably concerns him. And so that's his position. And with a witness who is here under subpoena, it's a position that he should probably identify himself to the Chamber. Indeed, he might even, in certain circumstances, be allowed to be represented by a lawyer, although he has no lawyer with him today, his lawyer having drafted the document that I would invite you in due course to read. That's part of the problem so far as Mr. Lilic is concerned. There is another part of that problem reflected in a filing that I think you have all seen. That comes from another party, that party wishing to have that matter dealt with in closed session, at least at this stage. And I would invite the Chamber, so far as Mr. Lilic is concerned and in order to plan ahead - and I think planning ahead is what's going to be required - to hear from Mr. Lilic so that you can understand his position, and then to hear from the other party. So far as that other party is concerned, I haven't yet seen the document filed here because I think the Chamber made a decision over the weekend to delay serving it on the Prosecution and the amici until this morning. I have to say that I've seen a draft of it having been in discussion with the party concerned on Friday. In discussion with but having no part in the drafting of the document save to suggest to them that if they wanted the matter to be dealt with in closed session, they should put that on top of the document so it shouldn't be missed. So I would be grateful for the opportunity of seeing the document as finally filed, and I would suggest that once the Chamber is acquainted with Mr. Lilic's position and then acquainted with the up-to-date position of the other party, we can plan more confidently how to deal with that very important evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But before we go on, there's a more general matter which concerns the Pre-Trial Conference which didn't take place last week and must take place this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that must be taken into consideration. That will have to take place on Friday, I would anticipate, at the last possible moment of the week. I don't know if there's any extra time available for sitting this week. I suspect there isn't going to be. The other matter -- I mean, is Mr. Lilic going to tell us anything more than you've told us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Possibly -- possibly a little more, but I'm concerned that because it is in part a matter between him and the Tribunal, that he should set his position out. It's the witness coming in answer to a subpoena, saying -- well, not I want to set the subpoena aside but, "At present, I can't answer the full terms of a subpoena or the implied terms of this subpoena because of these problems that are outstanding." And of course, although the authorities are cooperating - and I'm delighted that they're cooperating, I'm delighted that they're now indeed prepared to be represented here and to send, later this week, I think, lawyers to assist the Chamber - Mr. Lilic may be require, or alternatively, we on his behalf may be assisted by the Chamber's observations or orders, if it's able to make them, in relation to Mr. Lilic's problem. I can tell you this, that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's hear the witness and we'll then consider the matter further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. Although he has been in -- will Your Honour just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, although I'm asking that the witness be allowed to speak to you directly, I should say that he's been, of course, with the Office of the Prosecutor over the last few days, preparing the proof of evidence that we hope will reflect evidence he can give in due course. It is by no means finally completed, and I'm quite sure that it's not going to be possible, given all the constraints of time, for his evidence to be started and completed this week. That's clear. So I would ask that his addressing you about his role as a witness doesn't in any way trigger the moment when he can no longer be in touch with us about the substance of his evidence for it will still be necessary for us to deal with him on those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're saying that even if we do start his evidence, we can't complete it this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not given the time constraints that there are and not given the priority that I have put on K34 being completed this week, for other reasons of which the Chamber will be aware, practical reasons, that I judge must have priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will hear Mr. Lilic on this narrow point. He need not be under any form of declaration for this. He won't be treated as a witness. I suppose one thing we'll have to consider is whether it's worth calling him at all in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whether it's worth calling him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're in Your Honour's hands, of course, but I know that he would like to make his position plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll certainly hear him on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that one of the problems is that the document which has been submitted on Friday -- and I am truly concerned that it hasn't found its way to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It has now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, good. It is translated, but actually the translation, for whatever reason, is itself not entirely easy to follow in parts. And for my part in particular, the discrimination that's made in the document between the various state bodies and federal bodies concerned is not entirely clear. I'm sure this isn't the fault of the original document; it may be a consequence of the translation, I just don't know. It will probably be easier to hear from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll hear Mr. Lilic, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While he's being brought in, to save time, so far as the other party is concerned who wishes to be heard in closed session, my information is that they have a representative here to address you today in respect of their filing, should you wish it, but he -- he may or may not be a lawyer, but he's not the lawyer that they would wish to have address you for purposes of full legal argument. And the paper that they've submitted, or the submission that they've made contains interesting arguments which require a little research, particularly the topic of state dignity, which you will have seen referred to. And they told me yesterday that they intend to send a lawyer possibly Tuesday or Wednesday so that that matter could be more fully ventilated with the assistance of their legal representations later in the week. All these -- all these matters, of course, mean that the start time for K34 may have to be accelerated or advanced if other matters are going to have to happen before the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, we're not going to ask you to make a declaration. If you'd like to take a seat. Mr. Nice, since this is a Prosecution witness, you may want to start the proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Lilic, you're not being invited to take the solemn declaration at the moment because you're here simply to explain your position to the Chamber so far as giving evidence generally is concerned. I have to tell you that the filing of yours dated the 19th of July - last Friday - did not find its way to the Judges before this morning's hearing so they have not yet had an opportunity to consider it, and it may be the easiest course for you to explain your position as to giving evidence generally and the constraints that you believe exist on giving evidence and how those constraints may, in due course, be lifted. If you could explain your position briefly to the Chamber, that would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LILIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nice. Mr. May, by your leave, may I inform you at least in a few sentences about the core of this problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LILIC
utterances.text: Mr. May, Your Honours, according to your order of the 5th of July that was handed over to me on the 11th of July through the District Court in Belgrade, I am before the Prosecution of the Tribunal as a witness. I wish to point out that my presence in The Hague is an expression of my respect for a UN institution, for the Trial Chamber, and for you personally, and my objection to the Trial Chamber is a product of the need to protect myself and my family from the very serious sanctions stipulated by the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, due to the fact that the Federal Ministry of Justice, the Federal Government, and the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not act in accordance with the recommendations that were handed over to Mr. Markovic, the federal Minister of Justice, by Mr. Nice on behalf of the Prosecution on the 4th of July, 2002 and about which there is an official document, and I'm sure that Mr. Nice can interpret that. I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to point out that I have no objections with regard to the work of the investigators and the prosecutors of the Tribunal. On the contrary, the understanding of the prosecutors of the seriousness of the situation that I happen to be in because of the rather strange, I would say, behaviour of the government of Yugoslavia, the authorities of Yugoslavia, and also the effort made by the Prosecution in order to redress every possible misunderstanding make it incumbent upon me to thank them for their understanding. The core of the problem is that, from Belgrade, there are no concrete or clear decisions with regard to the testimony or giving evidence or against it. At least, I'm not aware of any such decisions and no such decisions have been made available to me. Therefore, I have been compelled to address the Trial Chamber for these reasons. I personally believe that it is in the interest of my country and the people that I belong to that the truth be presented in public before this Trial Chamber regardless of whether it will bring personal benefit to someone or personal disadvantage to someone. I believe that the truth is beneficial to all. And motivated by that principle, I am going to testify before this Trial Chamber, publicly, without any special protection, so that it would be made available to all, and this would eliminate the possibility of any speculation. And I believe that in the future, this would encourage other witnesses to speak before this Trial Chamber. In order for this to happen, two decisions have to be made by the authorities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. First and foremost, that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should express their approval of my testimony, that they should agree to it. That prerequisite has been met, in my opinion, because your subpoena, your order was handed over through the District Court in Belgrade. And the Court is in charge of that, according to article 5 on the law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. And secondly, what is was even more important for me and which is the core of the problem that I'm facing, it is also necessary for the competent authority - I underline this - the competent authority in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should free me from keeping a state secret and military secret and also to make it possible to have the necessary insight into documents from that period. This is simply required by the special position that I was in from 1993 until the year 2000. I wish to inform you of the following as well: Last week in Belgrade, meetings of the National Committee for Cooperation with the Hague Tribunal were held and also the government of the Republic of Serbia, the government of the Federation, and also the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Except for the sessions of the government of the Republic of Serbia that were held, one was on the 9th of July and the other one was on the 18th of July, where this particular subject matter was looked into, not from a single other level of authority do I have any decision in writing, because it was not handed over to my lawyer. The decisions that were reached do not meet the necessary requirements for two reasons. First of all, they pertain only to the field of Kosovo and Metohija and only in part; and secondly, they were given by the institutions that are not really in charge in my particular case. The Supreme Defence Council, at their session of the 19th of July, did not even look into the possibility of freeing me from keeping a state and military secret, and that is the only competent authority in my particular case. The Supreme Defence Council only passed a decision that certain documents that were required by the OTP could be made available to the Office of the Prosecutor, and in view of the very clear consequences stemming from the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, practically the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia rejected the previously given approval for me to testify when your subpoena was handed over. This assertion of mine can be seen the best from the following fact: In Article 40 of the law on cooperation between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and The Hague Tribunal, it is explicitly stipulated that as regards all questions pertaining to my position as a witness, it is the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, rather, it's Article 97 that are relevant, and this article reads as follows: "A witness who would by his or her statement infringe upon the duty of preserving a state secret, a military secret, or an official secret until the competent authority --" and in my case it is the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- "frees him of keeping such a secret, cannot be heard as a witness." Or rather, Mr. May, if anybody in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were to file a report against me, if I did not have an appropriate decision of the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whose president I was when these documents were conceived of and the use of these documents before this Trial Chamber has to be approved by the Supreme Defence Council, then I would be accused of revealing state secrets, military secrets, or official secrets, and there are serious speculations in this regard already in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in certainly daily newspapers and in certainly weekly publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can just invite you to pause there, because some of this comes fresh to the Chamber, they not having had the chance, for administrative reasons, of seeing your paper in advance. Can I just summarise the position, and you'll correct me if I'm got it wrong and then add anything that you still need to add. The processes for freeing individuals of liability for revealing state secrets are in place and are being worked through in respect of your case and in respect of documents to which you may refer and we simply don't know at the moment the final position from the authorities on whether you're going to be free of liability in respect of particular documents. But regardless of that, you take the view that the only authority that can free you ultimately from liability is the Supreme Defence Council and its president, which is Mr. Kostunica. And therefore, what you are seeking and what you have so far not been able to obtain is an express approval by that body or by him to your giving evidence, and you are concerned for your vulnerability if that approval is not forthcoming; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LILIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that there can be no doubt about the efforts that have been and the time over which efforts have been made, this was the subject of correspondence between you and President Kostunica as long ago as the beginning of February of this year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LILIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, on the 22nd of January this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your having explained your position and I having summarised the position about your need for the approval of -- approval of the Supreme Defence Council or the president, and the Chamber now knowing that the mechanisms are in place and we are working our way through the procedures to deal with particular documents - we don't have a final view on particular documents from anybody yet - is there anything else that you feel you should add to the statement you've already made to clarify your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, only a few more sentences. I would not like the impossibility for me to testify about these matters that relate to state and military secrets be considered as contempt of court. This is my basic human right not to expose myself to criminal Prosecution in the forthcoming period. It is precisely for that reason that I kindly ask you, Mr. May and Their Honours the other Judges, to look into this matter. We have given a detailed explanation of this obviously quite complicated procedure. Bearing in mind the fact that I do believe that the institution of a witness before an international Court enjoys the highest standards of human rights and, according to Sub-rule 90(E), should make it possible for the competent authorities of Yugoslavia to make the appropriate decisions. Why do I insist on the signature of the president, Mr. Kostunica, and an appropriate decision of the Supreme Defence Council? Precisely because that is the highest body that adopted most of these documents that will possibly be discussed here. As far as I know, that is the authority that can free a person from keeping such a secret, and in my situation, this is a rather special thing. The document that I have filed with you gives a detailed explanation, and I thank you for your attention on this occasion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Lilic. Mr. Nice, the witness rightly referred to Rule 90(E) which, of course, is a privilege against self-incrimination. The witness would certainly have that. But I'm not sure that I by any means follow what you're asking the Trial Chamber to do. Practically, this is a matter which has to be sorted out by others and not, I would have thought, by the Trial Chamber. We would, of course, hear, if it was proposed to call witness now, as was proposed, we would hear the witness. We would, of course, have to inform him that he wasn't obliged to answer any questions which might incriminate him, although we would have a power to compel him to do so, but I suspect we would be more likely to tell him he didn't have to incriminate himself, and then we would see how we got on. But that might not be the most efficacious way of hearing the evidence. It may be more practical, it seems to me, speaking for myself, to adjourn the matter for it to be resolved elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I had in mind -- in a sense this is perhaps a happy fit with the reduced time we now have as a result of the loss of time last week. What I have in mind is that, the Chamber now knowing from his own lips the witness's position and having other material before it and the potential to hear legal argument later in the week when, incidentally, Mr. Lilic will still be present in the building, I think the Chamber at the end of that exercise, perhaps Wednesday or Thursday, may be in a position to make orders or, alternatively, to set a timetable within which the whole process of Mr. Lilic's obtaining release from liability may be considered in order that sooner, rather than later, he can give the maximum possible evidence, evidence that will be of extreme value to this Tribunal and will touch on documents of very great value. So I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, when you applied for the issuance of a subpoena, all of these matters were not laid before the Chamber. I have no recollection of being privy to all of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When we applied for a subpoena, we were at an earlier stage in our understanding of the position, both with the witness and with the authorities, and of course the position in relation to the authorities is and always has been that we are making the best possible efforts at all times in an unfolding position so far as their cooperation is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I don't see why this witness should be subject to the regime of a subpoena at this stage. I think it is essentially a matter between the Prosecution and the witness and his authorities, and I rather resent having been, I think, used in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I may say so, there's two entirely different issues there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that they're entirely different at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm saying I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Had all of these matters been laid before me, I would not have agreed to the issuance of a subpoena in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
